articles.title: Hand-wash a wool garment
tools: One wool knit with readable care instructions
A clean, reachable sink or basin and water
Mild detergent suitable for wool
Two clean, pale, lint-free towels
A flat drying space and a timer

cautions: Use non-sensitive text because audio can be overheard. An app or note may already sync through its own service; this is not a confidentiality guarantee. Voices and pronunciation may not match the text perfectly.

sources.title: Apple: Hear iPhone speak the screen, selected text, and typing feedback (iOS 27)
Apple: Select, edit, and move text on iPhone (iOS 27)

steps.body: Open an unshared practice note in Notes. Type one harmless sentence, such as the invented “The small boat crossed the lake.” Set a comfortable audio volume and check who can hear it. This exercise reads existing text aloud; it does not need you to dictate, record other people or upload a document.
steps.title: Choose a harmless sentence first

steps.body: Open Settings > Accessibility > Read & Speak. Turn on Speak Selection if it is off, and remember its starting state. You do not need to enable VoiceOver or Speak Screen for this task. If you prefer not to change the setting, read the short passage normally and stop here.
steps.title: Enable Speak Selection if you want to try it

steps.body: Return to the note. Double-tap a word to select it, then drag the selection handles to include the sentence. Tap Speak in the text menu. Follow the visible words as they are spoken. If Speak is missing, check that Speak Selection is on and text is selected. Start again with one typed word if adjusting the handles is awkward; a picture of words is not the same as selectable text.
steps.title: Select only the words you want to hear

steps.body: Let the short selection finish, or use the speech controls that appear to pause it. If the pace is unhelpful, return to Read & Speak and adjust Speaking Rate, then repeat the same sentence. Success is hearing only the intended passage at a usable pace. Restore the prior rate or turn Speak Selection off there if you do not want to keep your changes.
steps.title: Check the pace, then finish or pause

articles.summary: Have iPhone speak a short passage you select, adjust its pace and return to ordinary reading using iOS 27 Read & Speak. Allow about five minutes.
articles.title: Hear selected text on iPhone
tools: An iPhone running iOS 27
A short, non-sensitive sentence in an unshared Notes practice note
A suitable place for audio, or headphones you already use

cautions: The brief heating method is for already cooked commercial beans. Never substitute dry or home-canned beans. Do not taste food from a suspicious can.
Hot beans, liquid and cookware can burn. Stop and ask for help if opening the can or handling the pan is unsafe. The 10-minute estimate includes setup; it is not a required heating time.

sources.title: La Preferida: How to Cook Beans, canned-bean stovetop method
FDA: Are You Storing Food Safely?
FDA: Refrigerator Thermometers, Cold Facts about Food Safety
US Fire Administration: Cooking Fire Safety

steps.body: Read the label: this method is for fully cooked, commercially canned beans in liquid, not dry beans, home-canned beans or refried mixtures. Follow any different directions on your can. Reject a swollen, leaking, badly rusted or severely damaged can; do not open it to test the contents. Check the ingredients for allergens.
steps.title: Choose a suitable can

steps.body: Wash hands, clean the can’s lid and set out the pan and bowl. Open using the opener’s instructions, keeping fingers away from the cut rim and lid. If opening is difficult, get help before cooking or choose a safely handled easy-open pack with its own directions.
steps.title: Clean, then open carefully

steps.body: For the simplest version of La Preferida’s method, pour the beans and their canning liquid into the saucepan; this route needs no added water. Do not heat the can itself. Choose a pan with room to stir. A small can makes a manageable first attempt without adding another recipe.
steps.title: Put beans and their liquid in the pan

steps.body: Heat gently, stirring occasionally, until small bubbles show a light simmer. La Preferida’s canned-bean method then calls for 2–3 minutes at that simmer. Keep stirring occasionally. Stay beside the pan, with the handle turned away from the front; turn the burner off if you must leave. If it bubbles aggressively or starts sticking, lower the heat.
steps.title: Heat gently and watch the pan

steps.body: Turn the burner off and use dry oven mitts if the handle is hot. Spoon the beans into the bowl; let a spoonful cool before checking whether it suits your taste. They should be heated through without scorching. Serve plain for the easier option. Promptly refrigerate any unused beans in a covered container, following the label and the leftovers guide.
steps.title: Switch off, then serve

articles.summary: Allow about 10 minutes to turn ordinary commercially canned beans into a warm serving using La Preferida’s stovetop method.
articles.title: Heat cooked canned beans in a pan
tools: An intact can of ordinary fully cooked beans in liquid, with readable directions
Can opener if needed; clean spoon and saucepan
Stove, timer, dry oven mitts and serving bowl

cautions: Do not share private history, a location or contact information because it would make a good conversation starter. Respect a declined introduction without passing along the person’s reason.

steps.body: Think of a connection the two people may enjoy, such as drawing in the same area. You can introduce them without a shared interest: simply wanting to include a willing newcomer is enough. Avoid promising friendship, expertise, favors or anything on either person’s behalf. Use only details they have agreed you may share.
steps.title: Choose a small, accurate reason

steps.body: Check separately: “Would you like an introduction to someone else here who enjoys drawing?” For a remote introduction, first ask permission before revealing a private name or detail to the other person. When each is open to it, confirm the specific introduction: “Would you like me to introduce you to Sam?” A no, hesitation or no reply means leave it for now.
steps.title: Ask each person before joining the conversation

steps.body: Ask what name to use and whether the small connection is okay to mention. For a message introduction, ask each person if you may share their specific email address or add them to the named conversation. Agree the audience before starting a group message; willingness to meet is not automatic permission to pass on contact details. In person, no exchange of numbers is needed.
steps.title: Check the name, detail and contact route

steps.body: Once both want the introduction, keep it short: “Sam, this is Jo. Jo, this is Sam. You both said you’ve been drawing local buildings.” Use the agreed detail, or stop after the names. An optional opening is “Have either of you tried sketching the old station?” They can change the topic or keep the exchange brief.
steps.title: Name both people and leave a starting point

steps.body: Pause instead of asking each person to perform an introduction or exchange contacts. In a message, a closing such as “I’ll leave you two to say hello if you’d like” is enough. Success is a wanted introduction with only agreed details shared, not a lasting connection. The low-energy version is names alone, after both say yes.
steps.title: Let the conversation belong to them

articles.summary: Use about ten minutes to ask two adults whether they want an introduction and agree what you may share; replies may take longer.
articles.title: Introduce two people with permission
tools: A way to speak with each person separately
An ordinary reason the introduction might interest them

steps.body: Try a natural meeting in a shared space when neither person appears busy. Do not block a doorway, interrupt a call or follow someone to get their attention. If the moment does not happen, it is fine to leave this for another day.
steps.title: Choose a moment with an easy exit

steps.body: Keep it simple: “Hi, I’m Sam. I’ve just moved into the building and wanted to say hello.” Share only the location detail you are comfortable making known. Pause so the other person can respond, or leave it at a wave.
steps.title: Offer your name and one sentence

steps.body: If they seem happy to chat, ask something small: “Have you lived around here long?” You can also say, “I’m still learning where everything is.” Skip personal questions and let brief answers stay brief. An introduction does not require a phone number or an invitation inside.
steps.title: Ask one optional, ordinary question

steps.body: Say, “Nice to meet you. See you around,” and continue with your day. If speaking is difficult, a short note signed with a first name can work where notes are welcome. Success is a respectful hello, even if it never becomes a friendship.
steps.title: Close before it becomes hard to leave

articles.summary: Make a short, friendly first hello without creating an obligation.
articles.title: Introduce yourself to a neighbor
tools: A comfortable moment
Optional first-name note

cautions: Do not write, glue, tape or clip anything onto the original photograph. Leave stuck, damaged or unfamiliar photographic materials in place and seek a photograph conservator’s advice before attempting treatment.

sources.title: Library of Congress: Care, Handling, and Storage of Photographs

steps.body: Choose a photo you can already see without pulling it from an album or frame; use an existing digital copy if available. Keep the original unchanged. If a print needs handling, use clean hands, avoid its image area and work on a clean, dry surface away from food and drink.
steps.title: Start with one viewable picture

steps.body: Record the existing filename or a precise location such as “green album, page 6, upper picture.” Add a short visible description, such as “two people beside a striped chair,” to distinguish nearby pictures. Write in a separate note, never on the original, and do not attach a sticky note or label.
steps.title: Give the note a reliable pointer

steps.body: Use headings for People, Date and Place. Enter a name, date or place only when you know it, and explain the basis if useful: “Place: my old kitchen; I recognize the tiled wall.” Leave a field unknown rather than using clothing, appearance or a familiar-looking building as proof.
steps.title: Write only the details you know

steps.body: If you have a tentative memory, separate it: “Possibly summer 2004; my recollection, not confirmed.” Do not silently turn an estimate into an exact date. If someone has already identified a detail, note who supplied it and when. Keep personal context private; a caption does not need a whole biography.
steps.title: Keep uncertainty and recollection visible

steps.body: Look away, then use your note to locate the same photo. Correct a vague location and date the note so later changes have context. Your result is a findable caption with knowns and unknowns separated. With little energy, record the picture’s location and one reliable detail, leaving the rest blank.
steps.title: Check that the caption finds the picture

articles.summary: Spend about fifteen minutes connecting one old photo to a separate note of known details, while leaving guesses clearly marked.
articles.title: Label an old photo with a caption note
tools: One old photo you can already view, or an existing digital copy
Paper and pencil, or a private digital note
Its existing filename, album position or other findable location

cautions: This is a fresh-fruit, ready-to-eat yogurt and cereal assembly guide. It does not prepare homemade yogurt, raw grain, or a product whose label requires cooking.
The amounts make one recipe portion, not a recommendation about how much anyone should eat. Check all ingredient labels if you have an allergy.

sources.title: Iowa State University Extension: Yogurt Parfaits
FDA: Selecting and Serving Produce Safely
FDA: Safe Food Handling, Clean and Chill
FDA: Are You Storing Food Safely?
FDA: Food Allergies, What You Need to Know

steps.body: Read the yogurt and cereal labels for ingredients, allergens and storage directions. Dairy yogurt contains milk; cereal can contain wheat, nuts or other allergens. Choose foods you can safely eat and keep yogurt refrigerated until measuring. Wash hands with soap and water and set out clean tools.
steps.title: Check the foods and clean your tools

steps.body: Wash fresh fruit under running water before peeling or cutting, including a banana whose skin will be removed. Dry with a clean towel. Peel and chop the banana, or use the washed blueberries without cutting. Measure ½ US cup prepared fruit. This worked example uses fresh fruit, so no frozen-fruit thawing or cooking method is implied.
steps.title: Wash before preparing the fruit

steps.body: Put ¼ US cup fruit in the bowl, then add ¼ US cup yogurt. Repeat with the remaining ¼ cup fruit and ¼ cup yogurt. That uses ½ cup of each ingredient in total. The layers help spread fruit through the bowl; it does not need to look like a photograph.
steps.title: Build four measured layers

steps.body: Measure 1 tablespoon ready-to-eat cereal and sprinkle it on top. Serve immediately, as Iowa State directs, so the cereal still has some crunch. If the glass is awkward to fill, use a wide bowl. If layers mix together, the task still succeeds: each spoonful should contain fruit and yogurt.
steps.title: Add the cereal just before eating

steps.body: Put unused yogurt and prepared fruit back in the fridge and follow their package directions. Keep the fridge at 40°F or below. Any perishable serving left out must be refrigerated within 2 hours, or 1 hour above 90°F; discard it if safe handling cannot be established. Do not use taste or smell to judge that safety.
steps.title: Return unused chilled ingredients promptly

articles.summary: Make one cold layered bowl with fruit, yogurt and a crisp cereal topping. Allow about 10 minutes; the measured layers come from Iowa State’s parfait recipe.
articles.title: Layer a fruit-and-yogurt parfait
tools: ½ US cup prepared fresh fruit, such as chopped banana or washed blueberries
½ US cup refrigerated ready-to-eat yogurt; 1 tbsp ready-to-eat cereal
Clean bowl or wide glass, spoon, ¼-cup measure and tablespoon
Clean colander; knife and board if needed

cautions: Use this for a voluntary adult social discussion, not therapy, assessment or a workplace decision. People need not defend their reading speed, disclose personal experiences or agree with the group.
Avoid recording, posting attributed remarks or sharing someone’s written contribution without their permission. Use chapter or scene references rather than distributing copied book pages.

steps.body: Before meeting, confirm the title, the part you will discuss and whether spoilers beyond it are off limits. Set a finish time and ask what makes participation easier, such as questions sent ahead or a quieter setting. Someone who has not finished can listen or discuss only the agreed section. This is a conversation, not a reading test. A whole book is optional: one agreed chapter can give you plenty to talk about.
steps.title: Agree on the section and the finish time

steps.body: Choose an opening reaction, one question about a choice in the book and a closing reflection. For fiction, try: “What stayed with you?” “What did the main character risk by keeping that secret?” and “Did your view change by the end?” For nonfiction, ask which example strengthened or weakened the author’s argument. Note a chapter or scene for each, since page numbers differ across formats. Avoid questions that contain your preferred answer. You do not need to research the author’s private life.
steps.title: Prepare three questions with places to revisit

steps.body: Remind the group of the section, spoiler limit and ending time. Say that passing is fine and people can share a written thought if that suits the agreed format. Ask the opening question, then leave a little thinking time. Invite responses without calling on someone who has not volunteered. If nobody starts, share one brief observation from the book and ask what others noticed. You are offering a starting point, not delivering the definitive interpretation.
steps.title: Open with room to speak or pass

steps.body: Ask “What in that scene led you there?” or “Did someone read that moment differently?” Give room for disagreement without requiring a vote. If one person takes most of the time, try “Let’s pause there and hear another angle.” For a tangent, acknowledge it and return to your next question. If nobody remembers a detail, check the relevant passage or leave it uncertain. Do not turn a character’s experience into a request for someone’s personal disclosure. A question can remain unresolved.
steps.title: Use the text to deepen, not win, the discussion

steps.body: With a few minutes left, ask what people are still thinking about; anyone may pass. Briefly name two different ideas the group explored without declaring a winning reading. Thank people and finish when promised. Discuss another meeting only if the group wants one, without assigning reading or hosting to absent people. Success is a conversation people could enter or decline, with a clear ending. For a shorter version, use one chapter, one open question and a ten-minute conversation.
steps.title: Close with one thought people can take away

articles.summary: Prepare a few open questions and guide a small, willing group through a book conversation. Allow fifteen minutes to prepare and about thirty minutes together.
articles.title: Lead a short informal book discussion
tools: A small group that has agreed to discuss the same book or section
Your copy in any available format and a few private notes
An agreed meeting place or call and a way to check the time

steps.body: Put down the pencil and look at the drawing as it is now. Choose a visible stopping point, such as “outline finished; handle still blank.” This is about returning to the same drawing, so do not turn the pause into a plan for a whole new project.
steps.title: Finish the mark you are making and pause

steps.body: On a separate slip, write a short Done line that describes the actual state. Try “Done: cup outline and left-side shadow.” If you are working from an ordinary object, note its direction or where the light came from if that matters to you. A rough setup sketch can replace a photo.
steps.title: Record what is already on the page

steps.body: Add a Next line small enough to begin immediately: “Shade the inside of the handle lightly.” Point to the area in a tiny thumbnail on the slip, rather than marking the original just as a reminder. “Finish drawing” is harder to start because it hides the first action.
steps.title: Write one exact restart action

steps.body: Write the drawing’s subject or page number on the slip and keep it alongside the sketchbook in its usual place. Leave the original as it is; avoid sticking a label over the drawing. This task does not require sorting the rest of your supplies or buying a special folder.
steps.title: Keep the cue with the right drawing

steps.body: Look away, then use only the slip to find the drawing and point to where you would restart. Rewrite a vague cue while you still remember. The pause is ready when Done and Next describe this exact page. If time is very short, one line naming the page and next mark is enough.
steps.title: Rehearse the return without doing more

articles.summary: Spend about five minutes preserving the stopping point in an unfinished pencil drawing so the next session has one obvious place to begin.
articles.title: Leave a drawing ready to resume
tools: An unfinished ordinary pencil drawing
A separate scrap of paper or private note
Your usual place for this drawing

cautions: This is an etiquette guide, not a menu-by-menu app tutorial. Exit options and effects depend on the app and conversation; no notification, deletion or privacy outcome is guaranteed.

steps.body: Read the recent conversation for something you actually agreed to do, such as bringing a game to the next gathering. Decide whether you are leaving the chat, the activity, or both. These are separate decisions. Write down any practical detail you still need, without copying other people’s private messages elsewhere.
steps.title: Check for one unfinished commitment

steps.body: If someone relies on you for an agreed task, confirm how that task will be handled before leaving. Ask another person rather than assigning them a responsibility. For an informal chat with no shared work, there may be nothing to hand over. You do not need to invent a closing ceremony.
steps.title: Resolve only the loose ends that matter

steps.body: Try: “I’m stepping out of this chat. Thanks for the good conversations. I’ll still bring the game on Saturday, as agreed.” Remove the last sentence if it is not true. Offer another contact route only if you want those messages; avoid promising to keep up with updates you will no longer receive.
steps.title: Write a brief, accurate goodbye

steps.body: When ready, send your note and follow the current official help for your app and device to leave. Read any confirmation before proceeding. If the app does not offer leaving for this conversation, pause and check its documented alternatives. Do not assume an exit will be unnoticed or remove earlier messages.
steps.title: Use the app’s own leaving instructions

steps.body: Check the app’s displayed result rather than relying on the chat disappearing from a list. Keep any remaining agreed plan somewhere you can find it. You are finished when your participation status is clear and commitments are covered. With little energy, send a two-sentence goodbye and resolve only the essential handover.
steps.title: Check the result and remaining plan

articles.summary: Spend about ten minutes checking loose ends and preparing a short goodbye for an ordinary social group chat.
articles.title: Leave a group chat considerately
tools: The group conversation
A private note if you have an outstanding commitment
Your app’s current official help if you need exit instructions

cautions: Use only an ordinary permitted coin on your own work surface. Do not rub monuments, gravestones, public surfaces, borrowed artwork or fragile and valuable objects.

steps.body: Put the backing sheet on the flat surface, set the coin on it with the face you want upward, and lay thin paper over the coin. Choose an ordinary coin with a raised design, not a collectible or fragile object. Leave enough paper around it for your other hand to hold the sheet still.
steps.title: Set up one coin and two sheets

steps.body: Locate the rim lightly through the paper. Hold the sheet close to the coin on two sides without covering the area you will rub. Keep that grip while you work. If you cannot comfortably hold and draw together, ask someone to hold the sheet, or use a larger coin and a smaller rubbing area.
steps.title: Keep the paper and coin from sliding

steps.body: Tilt the pencil so the side of its graphite point touches the paper. Use light, short back-and-forth strokes across the hidden coin, working from one side to the other. The raised rim and details should appear gradually. Keep the pencil on the paper; pressing harder is not a substitute for a steady sheet.
steps.title: Use the side of the pencil point

steps.body: Lift the paper and compare the rubbing with the coin. Can you identify the rim and at least one raised feature? If the pattern is doubled, the coin or sheet probably shifted; try a fresh area. If the result is faint, start again with thinner paper or another light pass before lifting. If the paper tears, use less pressure.
steps.title: Lift only after one light pass

steps.body: Keep the clearest rubbing and add a small note about which side you used. Return the coin to its usual place and collect the scrap paper. One recognizable rim and feature are enough for this session. To compare techniques, make a separate second rubbing with lighter strokes rather than trying to realign a sheet you already lifted.
steps.title: Choose a result and clear the surface

articles.summary: Reveal the raised pattern of one ordinary coin with a pencil and a thin sheet of paper.
articles.title: Make a coin rubbing on scrap paper
tools: An ordinary coin you own or have permission to use
Thin plain scrap paper and a spare backing sheet
An ordinary graphite pencil
A firm, flat work surface

cautions: Keep both files until you have checked the result. A second file on the same device should not be your only plan for protecting irreplaceable work.

sources.title: Apple: Organise files in folders on Mac
Microsoft: File Explorer in Windows
Apple: Rename files, folders, and disks on Mac

steps.body: Start with a local document you own, such as a club poster. Check its contents and remember its filename and folder. Finish or save any changes already in progress, then close it. For a shared online document, follow that service or your team’s copying instructions instead.
steps.title: Identify the original you want to keep

steps.body: In macOS Finder, select the file and choose File > Duplicate. In Windows 11 File Explorer, right-click the file and choose Copy, open a different folder you own, then choose Paste. If any prompt asks to replace an existing file, cancel and choose a different destination.
steps.title: Create a separate working copy

steps.body: Name the new file something distinct, such as club-poster-working. Keep the original filename unchanged and preserve the copy’s existing file ending, such as .pdf. Note where both files live. Do not start editing until you can point to two separate files with different names or locations.
steps.title: Give the copy a clear role

steps.body: Open the working copy and confirm its name before editing. Make a small, reversible change appropriate to the document, save it and close it. Open the original separately and check that the change is absent. If the files are not behaving as expected, stop before making larger edits.
steps.title: Test with one small change

steps.body: Reopen the named working copy and continue your task. Success means you can locate both files and the original still contains its earlier content. This session makes an editing copy; arrange a separate backup for irreplaceable files. Apple’s linked Time Machine guide explains external-storage backups for macOS.
steps.title: Continue in the checked working file

articles.summary: Create and check a separate working file before changing an original you want to keep.
articles.title: Make a copy before editing

A second folder for the Windows route
The document’s usual editing app

cautions: This list is a communication tool, not prescribing or dosing advice. Do not start, stop, substitute or change a medicine or supplement based on this guide; ask the appropriate clinician or pharmacist about uncertainties.
Medical details are private. Do not put this list in a shared task board or public document. Do not delay urgent care to finish it.

sources.title: FDA: Create and keep a medication list for your health

steps.body: Write “Current medication list” and the date. Use paper or a familiar private note; a new app is not required. Start with headings for prescriptions, over-the-counter medicines, and vitamins or supplements. Include items you use only sometimes. Keep packages available for checking without mixing their contents.
steps.title: Put today’s date on a private list

steps.body: For each item, copy the name and strength exactly, along with the existing instructions for when, how and how much you use. Note the reason for use if you know it. Do not invent a reason or turn an unclear label into an instruction. A blank template is enough: “Name | strength | current instructions | reason | question.”
steps.title: Record each item from its label

steps.body: If your actual use differs from the written instructions, record that separately and tell the clinician or pharmacist. If two records disagree, write “needs checking” beside both versions; do not choose a dose yourself. Add known allergies and an emergency contact to the private record, or mark an uncertainty for discussion.
steps.title: Mark gaps for a professional to check

steps.body: Ask: “Can we check that this accurately records what I currently use, including nonprescription products?” Keep questions beside the relevant item. If reading labels or making the list is difficult, bring the original labeled containers to a clinician or pharmacist and ask for help assembling it. Do not transfer items into unmarked containers for this task.
steps.title: Bring the list to the conversation

steps.body: Check that every item has its own entry or an explicit question and that the date is visible. Record any change in your actual use promptly and date it, marking anything not yet checked with your care team as “needs checking.” Keep actual use separate from confirmed instructions and ask the clinician or pharmacist to reconcile any difference; recording a change does not mean it is safe or recommended. Keep an accessible private copy for appointments and show it to the appropriate clinician or pharmacist. You are recording information, not authorizing a medicine change.
steps.title: Save one version you can find

articles.summary: Spend about twenty minutes assembling a private, dated record of what you use, with uncertainties clearly marked for a US clinician or pharmacist.
articles.title: Make a current medication list for a clinician
tools: Labels or current records for items you use
A private paper list or familiar notes app
Your clinician’s or pharmacist’s contact

steps.body: Pick one track or movement you can play again without searching through a long program. Write its title and performer as shown by your source so you can find the same version later. Choose an ordinary listening setting and a comfortable volume. This is an enjoyment exercise, not a hearing test or a music exam.
steps.title: Choose something short and easy to replay

steps.body: On the first listen, notice what catches your attention: a repeating sound, a voice entering, a sudden quiet part, or a change in pace. Let the piece finish before writing three short impressions. Everyday descriptions such as “a low humming sound” are enough. You do not have to identify an instrument or decide whether your reaction is the correct one.
steps.title: Hear the whole piece without chasing labels

steps.body: Choose one impression to investigate: “Does that opening sound return?” or “What changes when the voice begins?” Avoid trying to track every part at once. On your note, leave three spaces labeled Beginning, Middle and End. These are loose listening landmarks, not claims about the composer’s formal structure.
steps.title: Give the second listen one job

steps.body: Listen again with your one question in mind. Add a phrase at each landmark, such as “soft opening,” “new beat under the voice,” and “opening sound returns.” Those are fictional examples, not features every piece has. Add a playback time if your player shows one and it helps you find a moment; leave it approximate if you are unsure. Mark “not sure” rather than inventing an instrument name.
steps.title: Replay and mark what you hear

steps.body: Write one sentence: “On the second listen, I noticed…” Add a question you might explore on a later listen if you want. Use the title, performer and any time note to return to the same moment. You are done with a findable observation, even if your two listens felt different. Short version: hear the piece once and write one sound you noticed. If this listening activity is uncomfortable or not enjoyable, stop or choose another activity.
steps.title: Finish with something you can find again

articles.summary: Listen twice to one short piece and record a few sounds you notice, without needing musical vocabulary. Allow about fifteen minutes.
articles.title: Make a listening note for one piece of music
tools: One short piece of music you can already play lawfully
Your usual playback device
Paper and pen, or a private note

cautions: Use only a new, harmless test file on your own Mac. A work-managed Mac, network destination, cloud-only item or unfamiliar disk needs its administrator’s or Apple’s specific guidance.
An existing local copy, local Time Machine snapshot, Trash recovery or document version history is not this external-disk test. Keep the disk connected and deliberately select its timeline.
Stop at any erase, format, partition, claim-backup, replacement, password or unfamiliar permission prompt. This guide does not change security settings or provide backup setup.
One successful file test cannot prove that all files are protected. Exclusions, cloud-only files, later failures and a lost or damaged backup disk need a broader backup plan.
articles.jurisdiction: General; macOS Tahoe 26, existing directly connected Time Machine disk

sources.title: Apple: Back up your Mac with Time Machine
Apple: Local snapshots are separate from backup-disk copies (macOS Tahoe 26)
Apple: Select a specific backup disk’s timeline (macOS Tahoe 26)
Apple: Restore items backed up with Time Machine (macOS Tahoe 26)
Apple: Rename one file without changing its extension (macOS Tahoe 26)
Apple: Open a folder by its pathname (macOS Tahoe 26)
Apple: Create a new Finder folder (macOS Tahoe 26)
Apple: Create, save and open TextEdit documents (macOS Tahoe 26)

steps.body: Connect the disk you already use for this Mac’s Time Machine backups. In Apple menu > System Settings > General > Time Machine, match the listed disk to that physical device and note its name and latest completed backup time. This exercise requires one configured external destination. If there is no configured disk, several destinations you cannot distinguish, a setup/unlock prompt or an error, stop. Use Apple’s linked backup setup/support instructions separately; do not erase, reconfigure or enter credentials to complete this test.
steps.title: Identify the existing external destination

steps.body: In Finder, choose Go > Go to Folder, enter ~/, and open your home folder. Choose File > New Folder and give it a unique name such as Backup test 2026-10-04, using today’s date and a suffix if needed. Keep it outside cloud-synced folders. In TextEdit, create a new document with two fictional lines: “Blue teapot 47” and “Backup test”, plus today’s date. Save it as Sample in the new folder; keep the extension TextEdit supplies. Close and reopen it to check both lines, then close it. Record the folder, filename and test text on paper.
steps.title: Create one new test file

steps.body: Choose Back Up Now from the Time Machine menu. Keep the external disk connected and wait until the backup finishes. Reopen Time Machine settings and check that the latest backup for the named external disk is later than your test-file save. Write that completed date and time on your note. Apple says these Settings dates do not include local snapshots. If the date has not advanced, the backup fails or you cannot identify the destination, stop without treating the test as passed. Starting a backup is not completing one.
steps.title: Wait for a completed backup on that disk

steps.body: After the backup completes, select only the new Sample file in Finder and press Return. Change its base name to Sample-original, keep its extension and press Return again. Confirm Sample-original opens with both lines, then close it. Check that no file with the old Sample name remains in that test folder. Do not move anything to Trash or rename a valuable existing document. The old name is now a vacant restore destination; the newly named original remains available for comparison.
steps.title: Preserve the original under another name

steps.body: Keep the test folder open in Finder. In the Time Machine menu, hold Option and choose Browse Other Backup Disks; identify and select the same external disk. Stop if you cannot select it unambiguously. Use the backup timeline or arrows to select the completed backup you recorded, after the file was saved and before it was renamed. Wait if the backup is still loading. Locate Sample inside the test folder, select only that file and click Restore. Apple restores to its original location. Cancel any replacement or unexpected permission prompt; do not overwrite anything.
steps.title: Restore from the named disk’s timeline

steps.body: Back in the test folder, open the restored Sample and the preserved Sample-original separately. Confirm both contain exactly the two test lines and date you recorded, with no missing text. Record disk name, backup time, restore date and pass or the specific failure. Success is a completed external backup and this one separately restored file matching its original. It does not verify every file or full-Mac recovery. Leave both test files for now. Eject the backup disk before unplugging it. Low-energy route: do the first two steps now and resume later; record “not yet tested” until the restore passes.
steps.title: Compare the recovered content

articles.summary: Use an already configured external Time Machine disk to back up a harmless file, restore it beside a preserved original, and compare the contents. Allow twenty active minutes plus the backup’s variable waiting time.
articles.title: Back up and restore one test file on a Mac
tools: A Mac running macOS Tahoe 26 with Time Machine already configured for one directly connected external disk
That known disk already available without setup or password prompts, and the Time Machine menu already visible
TextEdit, Finder and a private paper note; no new purchase

steps.body: Write the person’s name and a possible occasion, if there is one. Keep the note somewhere private so a surprise stays optional. You can make an ideas list without deciding to buy anything, setting an obligation or collecting information the person has not chosen to share.
steps.title: Choose one person and an occasion

steps.body: Add two or three ordinary clues from conversation: a favorite author, a craft they enjoy or a color they mentioned liking. Include a short context, such as “wanted to try sketching buildings.” Separate direct comments from your own guesses, and avoid noting sensitive personal details.
steps.title: Record what they actually said

steps.body: For each clue, write a small option rather than a product order. A drawing interest might suggest a handmade sketchbook cover, shared sketching time or asking which supplies they already use. Include a no-purchase option if one fits. Do not assume an interest means they want more equipment.
steps.title: Make a few different possibilities

steps.body: Add questions that could matter before choosing: do they already own it, enjoy surprises or prefer choosing themselves? Leave a space for their answer rather than investigating private accounts or asking others for sensitive details. If a size or specification matters, plan to ask the person directly.
steps.title: Keep open questions visible

steps.body: Choose up to three ideas and note what you would need to check before acting. Date the entry so you can revisit old assumptions. You are finished when the note offers possibilities and clearly marked unknowns. With little energy, save one real clue and one possible thoughtful gesture; no purchase is needed.
steps.title: Keep only a useful handful

articles.summary: Spend about 15 minutes recording a few thoughtful possibilities without shopping or promising a gift.
articles.title: Make a private gift-ideas note
tools: A private note or notebook
A few things the person has actually mentioned

steps.body: Write three things the space needs to support, such as working at a desk, storing a bicycle or doing laundry. Think about the actual objects and routines involved. Keep the list short enough to use during one viewing rather than preparing questions about every possible home.
steps.title: Start with an ordinary day

steps.body: Read the listing and mark answers already stated. Copy the exact wording of anything important but unclear, such as “shared facilities.” Turn each gap into a specific question: “Who uses the laundry area, and how is access arranged?” Do not treat a photograph as an answer about daily use.
steps.title: Separate known details from gaps

steps.body: Add practical questions that affect your routine: which furniture stays, where parcels are received, whether a desk can go in the intended spot, or when the shared garden is used. Ask permission before photographing rooms. Keep this list focused on the property’s use and layout.
steps.title: Ask about how the space works

steps.body: Put a blank line beneath each question and mark your three priorities. Add columns for “shown to me,” “told to me” and “still unclear” if comparing several homes. A simple example is: “Bicycle location: space shown beside entrance; access arrangement still to ask.”
steps.title: Give answers a place to go

steps.body: Read silently or aloud, whichever suits you. Check that each question asks one thing and can be answered without explaining your entire life. Put the listing name and viewing date at the top. Your list is ready when your priorities have answer spaces. For a low-energy version, take just the three questions that could change your interest.
steps.title: Read through the questions once

articles.summary: Spend about 15 minutes preparing practical questions for a viewing; allow separate time for the visit and replies.
articles.title: Make a rental viewing question list
tools: The property listing
A private note or paper
Your own daily-routine priorities

cautions: A reading note records your understanding of a source; it does not verify every claim in that source. Keep attribution with quotations or paraphrases if you later use the material elsewhere.

steps.body: Pick a paragraph, a few pages or a short chapter you have already read. Write the title and author, plus the page number or section heading. If your format has no stable page numbers, describe the section. Keep the location accurate enough that you can return without rereading the whole work.
steps.title: Choose a small finished section

steps.body: In one or two sentences, explain what the section says in language you would use when telling someone about it. For a story, note a choice or change you noticed. For nonfiction, describe one idea. Leave out a detail you cannot remember rather than filling it in.
steps.title: Put the passage aside and write one idea

steps.body: Return to the passage and check whether your note changes the meaning or misses an important condition. Rewrite wording that follows the original too closely. If an exact short phrase matters, put quotation marks around it and record its location. Keep copied words visibly separate from your own explanation.
steps.title: Compare your note with the original

steps.body: Label a sentence “My thought” or “Question.” For example: “My thought: I want to compare this with the earlier chapter.” This separates the work’s claim from your reaction. A question can remain unanswered; you do not need to turn a small reading note into another research project.
steps.title: Add your own response on a separate line

steps.body: Read only the note. Can you tell what you read, which idea mattered and where to find it again? Correct any vague “this” or “they.” Save it with a recognizable title. With little energy, keep one sentence and its page or section; that is a useful finished note.
steps.title: Check that the note stands on its own

articles.summary: Spend about ten minutes recording one idea from something you have read, using your own words and a location you can revisit.
articles.title: Make a short reading note
tools: A short passage you have already read
Paper or a private note
The work’s title and author, where given

cautions: This organizing list is not an insurance inventory, valuation, ownership record or claim document. Keep private identifiers, access codes and sensitive records out.

steps.body: Pick a reachable place or ordinary item group, such as spare cables, picnic supplies or board games. Write a title and today’s date. Keep the first session to what you can see without moving heavy objects. This is a finding-things list; leave valuables and personal records outside its scope.
steps.title: Choose one small group to record

steps.body: Write Item, Quantity and Location. Add a short identifying detail only when similar things could be confused. An illustrative row is “Blue picnic blanket; one; hall cupboard, lower shelf.” Use words you would naturally search for, rather than creating codes you will have to decode later.
steps.title: Make three useful headings

steps.body: Take one item at a time and write its row. Count matching items rather than estimating from a closed container. Mark an uncertain count as unchecked. Keep an item where it is after noting it, and leave another person’s belongings alone unless they want to help record them.
steps.title: Record what you can actually see

steps.body: Choose a row, look away from the storage area, then use only the note to find that item. If “cupboard” is too vague, add the room and shelf. Correct the row while the location is fresh. A description is useful when it leads you back without opening every box.
steps.title: Test one location description

steps.body: Save the note with a recognizable name, or put the paper somewhere you will remember. Update a row when an item moves or the quantity changes. Success is a short list you can use, not a complete record of the home. With little energy, record and test three items only.
steps.title: Keep the list small and findable

articles.summary: Spend about fifteen minutes recording a small group of ordinary belongings so you can find them again.
articles.title: Make a simple household item inventory
tools: Paper and a pen, or a note you already use
Access to one reachable shelf, drawer or storage box

cautions: Use only material you may include. Avoid confidential work and personal information in a practice deck. Slideshow mode on your own computer does not itself share or publish the presentation.

sources.title: Google Workspace Learning Center: Create your first presentation in Slides
Google Docs Editors Help: Present slides (computer)

steps.body: Finish this sentence: “After this, I want the listener to understand…” Choose a small idea, not a whole subject. Invented example: “Our drawing group could try a five-minute warm-up.” Draft three lines: the suggestion, one concrete example and the next step. These are your three slides, not three unrelated topics.
steps.title: Write the one point before opening a deck

steps.body: In Google Slides on your computer, start a new presentation. Click Untitled presentation and give it a useful name, such as Drawing warm-up proposal. Keep a simple theme. Fill the first slide’s text boxes with the idea. Use New slide twice to add two more slides; choose a suitable Layout for each.
steps.title: Create and name a plain presentation

steps.body: Slide 1: “Try a five-minute warm-up.” Slide 2: “Draw the same mug twice,” with a simple shape or your own harmless sketch if useful. Slide 3: “Try it once at the next session?” Keep only a short line or two on each. This is a fictional proposal, not a claim that the exercise improves health or learning.
steps.title: Give each slide one job

steps.body: Select the first slide and click Slideshow. Use the arrow keys to move through all three, speaking the explanation in your own words. Press Esc to return to editing. If a slide is cramped or hard to read, remove words and enlarge the remaining text. Do not shrink everything to fit a paragraph.
steps.title: Rehearse from the first slide

steps.body: Run through the slides again. Can you explain the point, show the example and end with one clear next step without reading a wall of text? Check spelling and slide order. The result is a rehearsed draft; sharing, publishing and presenting to a real audience are separate choices. For an easier first pass, rehearse three paper cards using the same outline.
steps.title: Check the point, example and ending

articles.summary: Turn one modest idea into three readable slides and rehearse them on your own computer. Allow about twenty minutes in desktop Google Slides.
articles.title: Make a three-slide explanation in Google Slides
tools: Desktop Google Slides in an existing account
One ordinary topic you know
Paper or a note for a three-sentence outline

steps.body: Choose a concrete result, such as a four-line poem, a one-page collage or three sketches of the same cup. Replace “learn photography” with something you could show or describe when finished. Write one sentence: “I will make three pictures of objects on my desk.”
steps.title: Name one small finished thing

steps.body: Choose a short making session, a few materials and one intended use, such as keeping the work for yourself. Check what you already own. If the idea needs new supplies, shrink it or choose a substitute before buying anything. The twenty-minute estimate covers planning and starting, not every possible project.
steps.title: Set limits that fit this attempt

steps.body: For a collage, write: choose five scraps, arrange them on one page, then attach them. Keep research and setup small enough that making can begin today. Circle the first action you could do in two minutes. If every action still sounds large, make the finished thing smaller.
steps.title: Break the work into three visible actions

steps.body: Set a simple stopping point: “One page arranged and attached, even if some spaces remain.” Put optional ideas on a separate later list. Choose one practical check, such as whether the poem can be read aloud or all three sketches are on the page. Avoid adding new requirements halfway through.
steps.title: Decide what will count as enough

steps.body: Do the first two-minute action now. If you continue, work toward the stopping point you chose. If you pause, write the exact next action beside the materials. Success is a bounded plan with a real start; after finishing, choose whether to make another version or leave this one complete.
steps.title: Start, then leave a clear cue

articles.summary: Turn a creative idea into one small thing you can finish with the time and materials you have.

cautions: This is a general service-booking script. If a call requests information or payment you did not expect, pause and clarify through the business’s official contact route.

steps.body: Choose the ordinary service you want, such as a haircut, and note two or three times you could attend. Check the business’s own contact details and calling hours. Keep your calendar and notes nearby. The estimate is for preparation and a short call; waiting on hold may take longer.
steps.title: Write your request and availability

steps.body: Try: “Hello, I’d like to book a haircut. Do you have an appointment on Tuesday afternoon or Thursday morning?” If you reach voicemail, leave a brief request, your name and a callback number you are comfortable sharing. Do not assume the appointment is booked until someone confirms it.
steps.title: Start with one clear sentence

steps.body: Before agreeing, ask how long the appointment is expected to take, where to go, the price and any cancellation conditions. Ask about any practical access arrangements you need. If the offered time does not work, say so and ask for another. You can also say you will check and call back.
steps.title: Check what the offered slot includes

steps.body: Say the service, date and time, including the day of the week: “That’s a haircut on Thursday 8 October at ten in the morning, at the High Street branch?” Check the month or time zone if either could be unclear. Ask what you should bring, if anything.
steps.title: Read the details back aloud

steps.body: Record the business, location, appointment time and contact number. Add any preparation or cancellation note and a useful reminder. Check any confirmation against what was said. You are done when you can explain when and where to arrive; if there is a mismatch, contact the business to clarify.
steps.title: Put the confirmed details in your calendar

steps.body: Gather only the things you regularly take with you: perhaps keys, a transit pass and a reusable bag. Leave occasional equipment out for now. If you share a home, use your own items rather than reorganizing someone else’s belongings.
steps.title: Start with what you keep searching for

steps.body: Walk through your usual arriving-home routine. Pick a reachable place near where you naturally put things down, such as a shelf beside your bag. Try reaching it while seated if that matters for you. A spare bowl or shoebox lid works; this is not a shopping assignment.
steps.title: Choose a spot you already pass

steps.body: Place the items in the tray with enough room to see them. Put outgoing things, such as a library book, beside it in a separate “take next time” spot. Keep personal documents and visible address labels somewhere private instead of in a shared entrance.
steps.title: Give each item a clear space

steps.body: Pick up your essentials, then put them back. Can you collect everything without rummaging? Move the tray if the route feels awkward. For a low-energy version, make a home for just the item you lose most often. Try it for three departures before adding more items.
steps.title: Rehearse leaving and returning

cautions: If there is a real or suspected fire now, stop planning. Use a safe way out, stay out and call 911. Never enter smoke to test a route.
If heat, smoke or flames block all escape, stay in a room with the door closed, call 911 and give your location; follow emergency instructions.

This is general US preparation, not a building-code inspection, high-rise evacuation protocol, escape-ladder lesson or personalized assisted-evacuation plan. Obtain building-specific and fire-department advice for unresolved routes or support needs.

sources.title: US Fire Administration: Home Fire Escape Plans
US Fire Administration: Fire Safety for People with Disabilities
US Fire Administration: Fire Escape Plan Pictographs
American Red Cross: Home Fire Preparedness
American Red Cross: What To Do If a Fire Starts
American Red Cross: Fire Prevention Week, September 29, 2026

steps.body: Set aside a calm session with everyone who lives with you. Use paper or an accessible note. If you rent or share a building, get its current fire-evacuation instructions from management; your household plan must fit the building. For a high-rise or unclear evacuation instructions, work through the building-specific plan with management and the local fire department before rehearsing. Do not adapt a generic house drill yourself.
steps.title: Start before there is an emergency

steps.body: Sketch each level, label rooms, and mark doors and windows. In each room, identify two ways out, then trace where they lead. A window drawn on paper is not automatically a usable exit. Ask the local fire department for planning help if a second route is unclear, an exit is inaccessible, or the route would need climbing equipment. Do not invent a safe exit to finish the drawing.
steps.title: Map the home you actually have

steps.body: In normal, safe conditions, walk the routes you can use without climbing or taking risks. Keep doors, windows and exit paths clear; report stuck or blocked exits to management and seek fire-department advice. Discuss who may need assistance, including guests, and whether everyone can detect the alarm. Ask the fire department about a plan matched to mobility, hearing, vision or other needs. Do not assume a person can use stairs or a window.
steps.title: Check routes and individual needs

steps.body: Pick a specific place a safe distance from the building that everyone can recognize and reach. Mark it on the plan and say it aloud: “We meet at [our agreed place].” Agree how to contact each other if separated. In a real fire, leave belongings behind; once out, stay out and call 911 from safety. Tell responders if someone is missing. Never go back for a person, pet or possession.
steps.title: Choose one outside meeting place

steps.body: Plan the practice together, using your building's guidance where relevant. Follow the smoke-alarm manufacturer's test instructions, or use an agreed spoken practice signal. Rehearse ordinary safe exit routes to the meeting place; do not use real smoke or fire, climb out of windows, rush on stairs, or call 911 as a drill. If a route or assistance plan does not work, stop and get fire-department help before treating it as solved.
steps.title: Practice the agreed plan safely

steps.body: At the meeting place, ask each person to describe their routes and what they would do if separated. Correct the map and record unresolved questions with a next action, such as contacting the local fire department's non-emergency number. Keep the plan accessible to the household, not publicly posted online. Practice at least twice a year and review it when the home or household needs change. A rehearsal cannot certify a home as fire-safe.
steps.title: Keep a plan everyone can explain

articles.summary: Plan usable routes and an outside meeting place with your household, then rehearse safely. Allow 30 minutes for a first session; building or accessibility questions may take longer.
articles.title: Make and practice a US home fire-escape plan
tools: Paper and pen, or an accessible private note
Current building evacuation instructions, if applicable
Local fire-department non-emergency contact for planning questions

steps.body: Draw five adjacent boxes and label them 1 to 5 underneath. Leave box 1 as bare paper. Use the same pencil throughout so the comparison is about how you make marks, not about buying a set of pencils.
steps.title: Make five little boxes

steps.body: Shade box 5 with several overlapping passes of short, close strokes. Use steady, comfortable pressure rather than gouging the paper. Stop at a dark tone your pencil can make without crushing its point. The darkest sample does not need to be pure black.
steps.title: Establish the darkest sample

steps.body: Give box 3 a medium layer of strokes. Make box 2 lighter than 3 and box 4 darker than 3, adding passes gradually. Compare neighboring boxes in the same light. If 3 and 4 look alike, darken 4 a little; if 2 is too dark, lighten it with an eraser or redraw the strip. Aim for five distinguishable tones, not exact scientific intervals.
steps.title: Fill three clearly different middle tones

steps.body: Below the strip, draw a wide diamond for the box’s top. From its left, bottom and right points, draw equal-length lines straight down. Join the three new lower endpoints in a V. Shade the top to match sample 2, the left face to match 3 and the right face to match 5. Keep the faces separate; this is a simple tone-matching exercise, not a lighting formula.
steps.title: Use the strip on a three-face box

steps.body: Hold each shaded face near its strip sample and look for a similar lightness. Add a light pass only where needed. Write which pencil you used and keep the strip with the drawing. Success is five readable samples and three different box faces. For a shorter session, make only samples 1, 3 and 5; expand to five when you want a closer comparison.
steps.title: Check the matches before adding more

articles.summary: Create five shades from paper-white to your pencil’s dark tone, then use three of them on one small drawn box.
articles.title: Make and use a pencil value strip
tools: Scrap drawing paper
One ordinary graphite pencil
An eraser and straight edge if available

cautions: These steps cover text size on iOS 27. Supported apps can respond differently; this setting does not promise to enlarge every item on the screen.

sources.title: Apple: Make text easier to read on iPhone (iOS 27)

steps.body: Open a short, non-sensitive note in Notes on your iPhone running iOS 27. Read a sentence at your usual distance and notice what you would like to change. Pick an ordinary example, such as a hobby supplies list, so you can compare the same text afterward.
steps.title: Choose a familiar reading sample

steps.body: Open Settings, then Accessibility > Display & Text Size > Larger Text. Notice the slider’s starting position before moving it. This control sets a preferred size for supported apps, including Notes and Settings. Leave the other display controls alone while you test this one change.
steps.title: Find the text-size control

steps.body: Drag the slider a little toward larger text, then pause to read the sample shown. If the available range is still too small, turn on Larger Accessibility Sizes and try the additional sizes. Choose what you can comfortably read, rather than automatically choosing the largest setting.
steps.title: Try one larger setting

steps.body: Return to your note and read the same sentence. Then look at a familiar Settings screen. Can you read the text and find the controls you need? Scroll if necessary. A different app may not respond the same way; check its own text options if needed.
steps.title: Check the screens you actually use

steps.body: If the result feels awkward, return to Larger Text and move the slider back toward its earlier position. Stop when your two test screens are usable for you. With little energy, changing one slider and checking one note is a complete first attempt; you can revisit it later.
steps.title: Keep the useful change

articles.summary: Spend about five minutes trying a larger text size and checking two familiar screens on iOS 27.
articles.title: Make iPhone text easier to read

A short ordinary note to read

cautions: An ISBN helps identify a publication; it does not confirm a particular copy’s condition, availability or seller reliability. The examples are real publisher-listed editions, not purchase recommendations.

sources.title: International ISBN Agency: ISBN assignment
Penguin: Pride and Prejudice, paperback, ISBN 9780141439518
Penguin: Pride and Prejudice, hardback, ISBN 9780141040349

steps.body: Start with the book or requested edition. Look for ISBN on its copyright page or the publisher’s details page. Note the title, author and format beside it. If someone needs a particular translation or revision, get that requirement too; a title alone may fit several books.
steps.title: Find the identifier for the edition you need

steps.body: Copy every digit into the library catalogue’s search or use the publisher’s listing. A real example is Jane Austen’s Pride and Prejudice, Penguin Classics paperback, ISBN 9780141439518. Open the full record and inspect its details rather than relying on the search result’s cover image.
steps.title: Search the complete ISBN

steps.body: Compare the result with your note. Penguin’s hardback edition of the same title uses 9780141040349, so it is not the paperback example above. Different formats and revised editions can have different ISBNs. A reprint with unchanged text, binding and publisher can retain its ISBN; the number does not identify one individual copy.
steps.title: Match the number and format together

steps.body: Save the matching title, author, format and ISBN together. You are done when the details agree with the edition you need. If numbers disagree or a listing mixes formats, ask the librarian or seller to confirm the actual copy before requesting it. If no ISBN is available, give staff the title-page and edition details instead.
steps.title: Keep a matching record or ask about a mismatch

articles.summary: Use a book’s identifier and format together so a familiar title does not lead you to the wrong edition.
articles.title: Match a book edition using its ISBN
